name: Spaghetti carbonara
description: Pasta from four ingredients: guanciale, eggs, pecorino and pepper. There is no cream in it and never was.
instructions:
1. Bring a large pot of water to the boil and salt it properly — this is the only salt in the dish, since the cheese and the guanciale bring their own.
2. Put the guanciale into a cold pan and turn the heat to medium. The fat should render gradually and the pieces turn golden and crisp at the edges, about 6 to 8 minutes.
3. While the fat renders, beat the yolks, the whole egg, the grated pecorino and the pepper into a thick paste. Let it sit at room temperature so it does not seize when it meets hot pasta.
4. Cook the spaghetti a minute short of the packet time. Before draining, save a cup of the cooking water — the sauce will not come together without it.
5. Take the pan off the heat, add the pasta and toss it through the fat. Let the pan cool for twenty seconds — it should be warm, not hot.
6. Pour in the egg mixture and stir hard, adding pasta water a spoonful at a time until the sauce turns glossy and coats every strand. Serve immediately.

name: Ratatouille
description: A Provençal vegetable stew where each vegetable is cooked separately before they meet — otherwise it turns to mush.
instructions:
1. Fry the aubergine over high heat in two spoons of oil until the edges brown, then set it aside. Aubergine drinks oil instantly — do not add more, it gives it back later.
2. In the same pan, fry the courgette until golden, about four minutes, and add it to the aubergine. It should stay firm.
3. Fry the pepper until soft with a few charred spots and set it aside as well.
4. In the remaining oil, sweat the onion until soft, add the garlic and thyme and give it half a minute, until fragrant.
5. Add the tomatoes and cook them down over medium heat into a thick sauce, about twenty minutes. It should hold on a spoon rather than run off it.
6. Return the vegetables to the pan, season and warm them through together for ten minutes over low heat. Take it off, add the basil and let it stand — ratatouille is better warm than hot.

name: Borscht
description: A beetroot soup on beef stock where acid holds both the colour and the flavour. The beetroot is braised separately, never boiled in the pot.
instructions:
1. Cover the meat with cold water, bring it to the boil and skim. Simmer for an hour and a half at a bare tremble — a rolling boil turns the stock cloudy.
2. Braise the beetroot in a pan with a spoon of oil, the tomato paste and the vinegar, covered, for about twenty minutes. The vinegar is what keeps the colour.
3. Separately fry the onion and carrot until soft and golden.
4. Lift the meat out, pull it into pieces and return it to the stock. Add the potatoes and give them ten minutes — before any acid reaches the pot.
5. Add the cabbage, then after five minutes the beetroot and the fried vegetables. Give it five minutes more, add the bay and garlic and take it straight off the heat.
6. Let it stand covered for at least twenty minutes. Serve with sour cream, which softens the acid and pulls the flavours together.

name: Imeretian khachapuri
description: A round flatbread with the cheese inside rather than on top. The dough is made on matsoni, and there is as much filling as there is dough.
instructions:
1. Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm matsoni and leave it ten minutes to foam. No foam means dead yeast, so start again.
2. Add the egg, the melted butter, the salt and the flour. Knead a soft dough: it should stay slightly tacky, and no more flour goes in.
3. Cover it and leave it somewhere warm for an hour, until it has doubled.
4. Mix both cheeses together by hand until even and divide into four balls. Divide the dough into four as well.
5. Roll each piece of dough into a disc, set a ball of cheese in the middle, gather the edges to the centre and pinch them shut. Turn it seam down and roll it gently to about a centimetre thick.
6. Cook in a dry pan over medium heat for about four minutes a side, until dark spots appear. Brush the finished bread with butter.

name: Miso soup
description: A soup of dashi and miso that takes ten minutes. Miso must never boil: boiling takes out both the aroma and the point of it.
instructions:
1. Cover the kombu with cold water and set it over low heat. Bring it to the edge of a boil over about ten minutes and lift the seaweed out before bubbles appear.
2. Bring the water to the boil, add the bonito flakes, take it off the heat at once and let it stand for two minutes until the flakes sink.
3. Strain the stock through a sieve without pressing the flakes — pressed flakes turn it bitter.
4. Soak the wakame in cold water for five minutes; it swells several times over.
5. Warm the dashi, add the tofu and the wakame and hold it at a low heat for a couple of minutes.
6. Whisk the miso smooth in a ladle of the hot stock, stir it back in and take the pan off the heat immediately. Scatter over the spring onion.

name: Guacamole
description: Avocado, lime, onion and chilli crushed with a fork. No blender and no sour cream: both turn it into a dip rather than guacamole.
instructions:
1. Halve the avocados, remove the stones and scoop the flesh into a bowl. A ripe avocado gives under a finger without collapsing.
2. Add the lime juice and the salt straight away. The acid needs to reach the flesh before it starts to brown.
3. Crush with a fork to a coarse, uneven mass. Lumps of avocado should remain — that is the texture you want.
4. Fold in the onion, the jalapeño and the coriander, taste, and adjust the salt or lime. The tomato goes in last and gently, so it does not water everything down.
5. Serve at once. If it has to wait, press cling film directly onto the surface — air is what darkens it.

name: Tom yum goong
description: A hot and sour prawn soup where the balance is set at the end: fish sauce, lime and sugar go in to taste rather than by the recipe.
instructions:
1. Peel the prawns, leaving the tails on. Keep the shells and heads: the broth is built on them.
2. Fry the shells in the pot for a couple of minutes until bright orange, cover with the water and simmer fifteen minutes. Strain.
3. Return the broth to the heat, add the lemongrass, galangal and lime leaves and let them steep at a low simmer for five minutes.
4. Add the mushrooms and the crushed chillies, then after two minutes the prawns. They are done the moment they curl into a C — beyond that they turn rubbery.
5. Take the pot off the heat. Add the fish sauce, lime juice and sugar, stir and taste. Adjust a spoon at a time until sour, salty and hot sit where you want them.
6. Ladle into bowls and scatter over the coriander. Leave the lemongrass and galangal in the pot, or warn people not to eat them.

name: Dal tadka
description: A lentil stew finished by pouring sizzling spiced fat over it. That step is the dish.
instructions:
1. Cover the lentils with three cups of water, add the turmeric and simmer covered for thirty minutes, until the grains collapse into a soft mass.
2. Mash some of the lentils against the side of the pot and season. The consistency should be that of a thick soup.
3. Separately fry the onion until golden, add the tomatoes and cook until they break down into a sauce. Stir that into the lentils.
4. Heat the ghee in a small pan until it is just short of smoking. Add the mustard seeds; they should crackle within seconds.
5. Add the cumin at once, the garlic and chillies ten seconds later, the asafoetida twenty seconds after that. The whole thing takes under a minute and cannot be left alone.
6. Pour the sizzling tadka straight into the lentils — it should hiss. Stir once and serve with rice or flatbread.

name: Paella valenciana
description: Rice in a wide pan with chicken, rabbit and beans. It is never stirred once, and the crust on the bottom depends on that.
instructions:
1. Heat the oil in a wide pan and brown the chicken and rabbit on every side. This is not a five-minute job: it takes a good quarter of an hour, and there is no point rushing it — the flavour of the whole dish is laid down here.
2. Push the meat to the edges, put the green beans in the middle and fry them for a couple of minutes. Add the grated tomato and the paprika and cook until the tomato darkens and stops smelling raw.
3. Pour in the stock, add the rosemary, saffron and white beans, salt it noticeably harder than feels right and let it boil for ten minutes. This is the last moment you can correct the seasoning.
4. Scatter the rice in an even layer and level it once with a spoon. After that do not touch the pan again — no stirring, no smoothing.
5. Cook on a high flame for ten minutes, then drop to medium for another eight, until the stock is gone. The rice should be showing above the surface.
6. Turn the heat up for half a minute and listen: the moment the sound turns from bubbling to a dry crackle, take it off. That is the socarrat. Cover with a cloth and let it stand for five minutes.

ingredients.name: bomba rice, or another short grain

name: Moussaka
description: Aubergine, a meat sauce with cinnamon and a thick layer of béchamel, baked until it sets firm enough to cut.
instructions:
1. Salt the aubergine slices and leave them in a colander for half an hour, then pat them dry. Brush with oil and roast at 200 °C for twenty minutes until soft and golden.
2. Fry the onion until soft, add the mince and cook, breaking up the lumps, until every drop of water has gone and the meat starts to brown. Pour in the wine and let it cook away.
3. Add the garlic, tomatoes and cinnamon and simmer for twenty minutes. The sauce is right when a spoon drawn across the bottom leaves a track behind it.
4. Melt the butter, whisk in the flour and cook for a minute. Pour in warm milk in a thin stream, whisking without stopping, and cook to the thickness of soured cream. Off the heat, add nutmeg, the yolks and half the cheese.
5. Layer it up: potato, aubergine, meat sauce, aubergine again. Pour the béchamel over and scatter the rest of the cheese.
6. Bake at 180 °C for forty-five minutes until the top is golden. Let it stand for half an hour before cutting: hot moussaka does not slice, it slumps.

name: Phở bò
description: A clear beef broth with charred ginger and whole spices, rice noodles, and beef that finishes cooking in the bowl.
instructions:
1. Cover the bones with cold water, bring to the boil and let them go for ten minutes. Throw the water away, rinse the bones under the tap and wash the pot. This step is what buys you a clear broth.
2. Halve the onion and ginger and char the cut faces in a dry pan or straight over the flame until they blacken in patches.
3. Toast the spices in a dry pan until they smell, then tie them in muslin. Return the bones to the clean pot with the brisket, onion, ginger and spices, and cover with water three fingers above.
4. Simmer for three hours at the barest tremble. Skim for the first half hour. Lift the brisket out after ninety minutes and let it cool.
5. Strain the broth through a fine sieve and season with fish sauce and sugar. Taste it: it should be slightly saltier than pleasant to drink on its own, because the noodles will take their share.
6. Cook the noodles and divide them between bowls. Lay the sliced brisket and the raw sirloin on top. Ladle boiling broth over so it covers the meat, and serve the herbs, lime and chilli alongside.

name: Menemen
description: Eggs cooked into tomatoes and green pepper. They are never beaten and rarely stirred, or you end up with ordinary scrambled eggs.
instructions:
1. Slice the peppers into rings and fry them in the two fats for three or four minutes, until the edges start to darken.
2. Add the tomatoes, salt them and cook over medium heat for ten minutes. Wait for the oil to separate and glisten at the edges — that is the sign the water has gone.
3. Lower the heat, break the eggs straight into the sauce and scatter the pepper flakes. Stir slowly and only two or three times, leaving streaks of yolk.
4. Take it off when the white has set and the yolk is still loose: the pan finishes the job. Scatter over the oregano and the cheese.

name: Ceviche
description: Raw fish in lime juice with onion and ají. It marinates for minutes, not hours — longer and it is cooked through.
instructions:
1. Soak the sliced onion in iced water for ten minutes and pat it dry: the harshness goes, the flavour stays.
2. Squeeze the limes by hand rather than in a press: pressure on the skin releases bitter oils.
3. Salt the fish, mix it with the chopped ají and coriander, pour the lime over and leave it exactly three to five minutes. The edges turn opaque and the middle stays translucent.
4. Add the onion, toss once and serve at once with the sweet potato and corn. Pour the juice from the bowl into small glasses.

name: Mapo tofu
description: Tofu in a hot doubanjiang sauce with Sichuan pepper, which numbs rather than burns.
instructions:
1. Slip the tofu into barely simmering salted water for three minutes and drain it gently.
2. Fry the pork until browned and its fat has rendered, then push it aside. Add the doubanjiang and fry for a minute, until the oil turns red.
3. Add the garlic, ginger and black beans, warm for half a minute and pour in the stock. Bring it to the boil.
4. Slide the tofu in and simmer for three minutes without stirring — swirl the pan instead, or the cubes break up.
5. Slake the cornflour in cold water and add it in two goes, letting the sauce come back to the boil each time. Off the heat, scatter over the ground Sichuan pepper and spring onion.

name: Käsespätzle
description: Swabian egg noodles layered with cheese and buried under fried onion.
instructions:
1. Mix the flour, eggs, water, salt and nutmeg and beat the dough with a spoon for a good five minutes, until bubbles rise and it starts to string off the spoon.
2. While the dough rests, fry the onion in butter over medium heat until deep gold. That is twenty minutes, not five — the sugars need the time to caramelise.
3. Press the dough into boiling salted water through a spätzle grater or a wide-holed colander. They float within a minute; lift them out with a slotted spoon.
4. Layer them into a warm dish: spätzle, cheese, spätzle, cheese. The heat of the noodles melts it; no oven is needed.
5. Bury it under the fried onion and serve at once. The classic side is a green salad with a vinegar dressing, and it is a counterweight rather than a garnish.

name: Bibimbap
description: Rice under separately cooked vegetables, meat and an egg, mixed with gochujang right before eating.
instructions:
1. Marinate the beef in soy, garlic and a spoon of sesame oil for twenty minutes.
2. Blanch the spinach for thirty seconds, squeeze it dry and dress with sesame oil and a pinch of salt. Boil the sprouts three minutes and dress them the same way, with garlic.
3. Fry the carrot and the mushrooms separately, a couple of minutes each, seasoning each on its own. No need to wash the pan in between.
4. Sear the beef over a high flame for two minutes. Fry the eggs separately, leaving the yolks runny.
5. Divide the hot rice between bowls, arrange the vegetables and beef in sections, and top with an egg and a spoon of gochujang. Each person does the mixing.

name: Pierogi ruskie
description: Dumplings of potato and curd cheese, served with fried onion and soured cream.
instructions:
1. Pour the boiling water with the oil and salt over the flour, work it with a spoon and then, once it cools, by hand for eight minutes. Cover and rest it half an hour.
2. Fry two of the onions in butter to a deep gold. Half goes into the filling and half is kept for serving.
3. Mash the warm potato with the curd and the fried onion, and season generously. The filling has to be firm enough to hold its shape.
4. Roll the dough to two millimetres, cut discs with a glass, add a teaspoon of filling and pinch the edges dry — wet dough will not seal.
5. Boil in batches in a wide pot of salted water. Lift them out a minute after they float.
6. Serve with the rest of the fried onion and soured cream. Plenty of people fry the boiled pierogi in butter afterwards, which is equally correct.

name: Shakshuka
description: Eggs poached in a thick sauce of tomato and pepper with cumin and paprika.
instructions:
1. Fry the onion and peppers in the oil for ten minutes, until the pepper is soft and sweet.
2. Add the garlic, cumin, paprika and harissa and warm them for a minute — to the smell, not to burning.
3. Pour in the tomatoes, crush them and simmer for fifteen minutes. The sauce is ready when a spoon leaves a track on the bottom.
4. Make hollows with a spoon and break an egg into each. Cover and give it five to seven minutes: the whites set, the yolks stay loose.
5. Scatter over the feta and coriander and serve it in the pan with bread.

name: Feijoada
description: Black beans stewed with several cuts of smoked and salted pork, served with orange and greens.
instructions:
1. Boil the salted meat in fresh water for twenty minutes and drain: the last stage of getting the salt out.
2. Cover the beans with water three fingers above, add the bay, the ribs and the salted meat, and simmer for an hour and a half.
3. Add the belly and the sausage and give it another hour. The beans should be collapsing and the liquid thickening on its own.
4. Fry the onion and garlic until golden, add a ladle of beans, mash them and return it all to the pot. That thickens the stew and deepens it.
5. Fry the greens over a high flame for two minutes with garlic — they should stay bright green and crisp.
6. Serve the beans and meat with the rice, greens and orange segments alongside. Everyone builds their own plate.

name: Chicken tagine with preserved lemon
description: Chicken braised with preserved lemons and olives. The sourness comes from the peel, not the flesh.
instructions:
1. Grind the garlic, ginger, turmeric, saffron, chopped herbs, oil, salt and pepper into a paste. Rub it over the chicken and leave it an hour.
2. Spread the onion in an even layer over the base of the tagine or a heavy pan: it keeps the chicken off the bottom and becomes part of the sauce.
3. Set the chicken on top skin up, pour the water down the side, cover and cook over a low flame for forty minutes without lifting the lid.
4. Add the preserved lemon peel in strips and the olives, cover and give it twenty minutes more.
5. Take the lid off and reduce the sauce for five minutes if it is still loose. Check the salt only at the end: the lemon and olives have already provided it.

name: Goulash
description: Beef stewed with onion and paprika. There is as much onion by weight as meat, and it dissolves into the sauce.
instructions:
1. Sweat the onion in the lard over a low flame for twenty minutes, until soft and golden. It feels long and pointless, and it is where the sweetness of the sauce comes from.
2. Take the pan off the heat, add the paprika and caraway and stir. Half a minute later return it to the flame and add the meat.
3. Cook the meat with the onion covered for half an hour without adding water: it gives up its own. Only then pour in water to the level of the meat.
4. Simmer for an hour and a half. Add the peppers, tomatoes and garlic forty minutes before the end, the potatoes twenty-five.
5. Salt it at the very end and let it stand fifteen minutes before serving.

name: Fish and chips
description: Cod in beer batter with twice-fried chips. The batter lives on cold and on the gas in the beer.
instructions:
1. Rinse the cut potatoes of their starch, dry them thoroughly and fry at 140 °C for six minutes. They should turn soft but stay pale. Set them aside to cool.
2. Mix the flour, cornflour and baking powder. Pour in the ice-cold beer and whisk only a few strokes — lumps are fine, an over-mixed batter turns tough.
3. Dry the fish, dust it in plain flour and shake off the excess. Without that the batter slides off in the oil.
4. Heat the oil to 190 °C. Dip the fish, let the excess run off and lower it in, holding it for a couple of seconds so it does not stick to the bottom. Fry six minutes.
5. Lift the fish out and finish the chips in the same oil for three minutes, until gold. Salt them at once, while hot.

name: Wiener Schnitzel
description: Veal beaten to three millimetres, crumbed and fried in plenty of fat until the coating puffs away.
instructions:
1. Beat the meat between two sheets of film to three millimetres. Use the flat side of the mallet, not the toothed one: teeth tear the fibres.
2. Beat the eggs to an even liquid without foam. Salt the meat and coat it in flour, then egg, then crumbs.
3. Do not press the crumbs on. The coating has to sit loosely; only then will it lift and puff.
4. Heat a centimetre of fat to 170 °C and lower the schnitzel in. Fry two minutes, swirling the pan the whole time so fat washes over the top.
5. Turn it and give it ninety seconds more, to gold. Drain on a rack and serve immediately with a wedge of lemon.

name: Bacalhau à brás
description: Salt cod with matchstick potatoes and egg that binds everything without becoming an omelette.
instructions:
1. Poach the soaked cod for five minutes, cool it and pull it into flakes by hand, discarding skin and bones. By hand rather than with a fork: that is how small bones are found.
2. Deep-fry the potato matchsticks at 180 °C to a crisp gold, in batches. Drain on a rack and salt them.
3. In a wide pan sweat the onion in the olive oil for ten minutes until soft and sweet, adding the garlic for the last minute.
4. Add the cod and warm it through for three minutes, then tip in the potato and toss.
5. Take the pan off the heat, pour in the beaten eggs and stir without stopping for half a minute, until they turn creamy. Scatter over the parsley and olives.

name: Argentinian empanadas
description: Pastries of chopped beef, onion and egg. The filling is chilled cold, or the dough will not seal.
instructions:
1. Fry the onion in the lard over medium heat for fifteen minutes, until soft and translucent, without letting it colour.
2. Add the chopped beef, paprika, cumin and chilli and cook five minutes: the meat should only lose its pink, no more.
3. Season, take it off the heat and cool it completely, then refrigerate for at least four hours.
4. Fold the chopped egg, olives and spring onion into the cold filling.
5. Put a tablespoon of filling on each disc, wet the rim, fold it over and crimp it into the plaited repulgue, folding the corners over one another.
6. Brush with yolk and bake at 220 °C for twenty minutes, until browned.

name: Nasi goreng
description: Fried rice with a chilli and shrimp-paste base, sweet soy sauce and an egg on top.
instructions:
1. Pound the shallot, garlic, chilli and terasi to a paste in a mortar. It smells aggressive; that is correct, frying softens it.
2. Heat the wok and fry the paste in the oil for two minutes, until it darkens and the smell turns deep.
3. Add the chicken and fry three minutes, then the prawns and cabbage for two more.
4. Tip in the cold rice, breaking up the lumps with the spatula, pour in the kecap manis and fry over a high flame for three minutes, tossing constantly.
5. Fry the eggs separately until the edges are lacy and the yolks loose. Serve the rice with an egg on top, slices of cucumber and fried shallots.

name: Chicken adobo
description: Chicken braised in soy sauce with vinegar, garlic and bay. The vinegar is left unstirred for the first ten minutes.
instructions:
1. Marinate the chicken in the soy with the crushed garlic and peppercorns for thirty minutes.
2. Lift the chicken out, dry it and brown it skin down. Keep the marinade.
3. Pour in the marinade, water and vinegar, add the bay and sugar. Bring it to the boil and neither stir nor cover for ten minutes.
4. Cover and simmer for twenty-five minutes, turning the chicken once.
5. Uncover and reduce the sauce for five to ten minutes, spooning it over the chicken. Serve with rice.

name: Ukrainian borscht with pampushky
description: Borscht on pork ribs with aged salo crushed with garlic, and garlic pampushky alongside.
instructions:
1. Make a stock from the ribs: an hour and a half at a bare simmer, skimmed. Lift the meat out and pull it apart.
2. Braise the beetroot separately with a spoon of oil, the tomato paste and the vinegar, covered, for twenty minutes. The vinegar is what holds the colour.
3. Fry the onion and carrot until soft. Put the potatoes into the stock and give them ten minutes, before any acid reaches the pot.
4. Add the cabbage, then after five minutes the beetroot, the fried vegetables and the beans. Give it five minutes.
5. Pound the salo with the garlic and herbs to a paste and stir it into the pot. Take it straight off the heat and let it stand covered for twenty minutes.

name: Svíčková na smetaně
description: Beef in a purée of root vegetables with cream, served with dumplings, lingonberry and lemon.
instructions:
1. Lard the beef with strips of smoked fat laid along the grain. Bury it in the grated roots with the spices and vinegar and refrigerate for a day.
2. Dry the meat and brown it in butter on all sides. Lift it out.
3. In the same pan fry the roots from the marinade with the onion for twenty minutes: they should darken noticeably, which is where the colour comes from.
4. Return the meat, pour in the marinade and enough water to reach the vegetables, and braise covered for two hours over a low flame.
5. Take the meat out, remove the bay and blend the vegetables with the liquid until smooth. Pass it through a sieve: this is the step that separates a home svíčková from a restaurant one.
6. Stir in the cream, lemon juice and sugar, warm it without boiling and taste. Carve the meat across the grain and serve with the sauce, lingonberry and a slice of lemon.

name: Köttbullar
description: Meatballs on a panade of bread and cream, in a cream sauce, with lingonberry and mashed potato.
instructions:
1. Soak the bread in a hundred millilitres of the cream for ten minutes and mash it to a paste.
2. Fry the onion in butter until soft and cool it completely: warm onion starts cooking the meat.
3. Mix both minces with the panade, onion, egg, allspice and salt, and work it for five minutes until tacky.
4. Roll walnut-sized balls with wet hands and fry them in butter in batches, shaking the pan so they roll and colour evenly.
5. In the same pan whisk the flour into the remaining fat, pour in the stock and the rest of the cream, add the soy and cook five minutes to a sauce.
6. Return the meatballs to the sauce and warm them through for five minutes. Serve with mashed potato, lingonberry and pickled cucumber.

name: Koshari
description: Rice, lentils and pasta in one bowl under a vinegary tomato sauce and fried onion.
instructions:
1. Fry the onion in the oil over medium heat for twenty-five minutes to a deep brown, stirring. Drain it on paper; it crisps as it cools.
2. Boil the lentils for twenty minutes to soft but not collapsing, and drain.
3. Cook the rice in the onion oil: fry it two minutes, add water at one and a half to one and cook covered for fifteen minutes.
4. Boil the pasta and drain it. For the sauce, fry the garlic in a spoon of oil to gold, pour in the vinegar and let it reduce by half.
5. Add the tomatoes, cumin and chilli and cook twenty minutes to a thick sauce. Season.
6. Build it in the bowl in layers: rice, lentils, pasta, chickpeas, sauce, fried onion. The mixing happens at the table.

name: Tabbouleh
description: A parsley salad with a little bulgur in it, not the other way round. There is ten times more herb than grain.
instructions:
1. Rinse the bulgur and pour the juice of one lemon over it. Leave it to swell for fifteen minutes.
2. Wash the parsley well in advance and dry it thoroughly — an hour on a cloth is not too much. Strip the thick stems and chop it fine but without pulverising it.
3. Dice the tomatoes small and salt them separately: the juice they give up goes into the bulgur.
4. Mix everything with the juice of the second lemon, the oil and the allspice. Let it stand ten minutes before serving.

name: Ghormeh sabzi
description: Lamb stewed with a mountain of herbs, beans and dried lime. The herbs are fried until nearly black.
instructions:
1. Fry the onion with the turmeric until gold, add the meat and brown it on all sides.
2. Cover with water, add the beans and simmer for an hour.
3. Meanwhile chop all the herbs fine and fry them in the oil for twenty minutes, stirring. They shrink to a quarter and darken; that is correct. Add the fenugreek for the last two minutes.
4. Stir the herbs into the pot, prick the dried limes with a fork and drop them in whole. Simmer for another hour.
5. Crush the limes against the side of the pot, season and let it stand fifteen minutes. The sauce should be dark and thick, with oil separated on top.

name: Uzbek plov
description: Rice steamed over a zirvak of lamb, carrot and onion. It is never stirred once it goes in.
instructions:
1. Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and cover it with warm salted water for as long as the zirvak takes.
2. Render the tail fat in the pot until only crackling is left and lift it out. Brown the meat hard over a high flame.
3. Add the onion and fry it gold, then the carrot — and leave it alone for five minutes so it sets. Then stir and fry ten minutes more.
4. Pour in boiling water to the level of the contents, add the chickpeas, cumin, barberries, chilli and the whole garlic bulbs. Simmer for forty minutes: this is the zirvak.
5. Salt the zirvak noticeably harder than seems right: the rice takes it. Spread the rice over in an even layer with a slotted spoon, without stirring, and pour boiling water two fingers above it.
6. Cook uncovered over a high flame until the water drops below the rice. Gather the rice into a mound, pierce it to the base in several places, cover and give it twenty minutes on the lowest heat.

name: New England clam chowder
description: A thick clam soup with cream, potato and bacon. No tomato — that is a matter of principle.
instructions:
1. Scrub the clams and steam them in a cup of water, covered, for five minutes, until they open. Discard any that stay shut. Strain the liquor through muslin: sand settles in it.
2. Take the meat from the shells and chop it coarsely. Set it aside; it returns at the very end.
3. Render the bacon in the pot, add the butter, onion and celery, and sweat them for eight minutes until soft.
4. Stir in the flour, cook it two minutes, pour in the strained clam liquor and the milk, and add the potato, thyme and bay.
5. Simmer for fifteen minutes until the potato is soft. Crush a few pieces against the side: the soup thickens without more flour.
6. Pour in the cream, return the clams and warm through for two minutes without boiling. Check the salt and serve with crackers.

name: Nihari
description: Beef shin stewed overnight in a thick spiced gravy with marrow, bound with a wheat-flour slurry.
instructions:
1. Fry the onions in ghee to a deep gold, about twenty minutes. Set half aside for serving.
2. Add the ginger and garlic, the spices and the chilli, warm them a minute, then the meat and bones, and sear until the raw colour goes.
3. Cover with water three fingers above, bring to the boil, skim and cook on the lowest heat for four or five hours. The meat should fall apart at a touch.
4. Whisk the flour into a cup of cold water until smooth and pour it in as a thin stream, stirring constantly. Cook ten minutes: the gravy thickens and turns glossy.
5. Lift out the bones and set the marrow aside separately. Serve with the fried onion, matchsticks of ginger, coriander, green chilli and lemon — everyone adds their own.

name: Laksa lemak
description: Noodles in a coconut broth built on a rempah paste, with prawns and tofu. The paste is fried until the oil separates.
instructions:
1. Soak the dried chillies in boiling water for fifteen minutes, then blend them with the shallots, lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and belacan to a smooth paste.
2. Fry the paste in the oil over medium heat for fifteen minutes, stirring. It is ready when the oil starts separating and rising at the edges.
3. Pour in the stock, bring it to the boil and simmer ten minutes. Add the prawns and tofu for three minutes.
4. Add the coconut milk and warm it through without letting it boil hard. Season.
5. Divide the cooked noodles between bowls, ladle the broth over and serve the sprouts, cucumber and lime alongside.

name: Stamppot
description: Mashed potato crushed together with curly kale, with smoked sausage and a well of gravy.
instructions:
1. Boil the potatoes in salted water for twenty minutes. Seven minutes before the end pile the kale on top to steam.
2. Meanwhile warm the sausage in water for twenty minutes without letting it boil: boiling splits the skin and the fat leaves.
3. Render the bacon until crisp and set it aside, keeping the fat.
4. Drain, crush the potato and kale together with a masher, working in the hot milk, butter, bacon fat and mustard.
5. Fold in the crackling, divide between plates, make a well and fill it with gravy. Slice the sausage and lay it over.

name: Doro wat
description: Chicken in a thick berbere sauce, built on a kilo of onion cooked dry until it disintegrates.
instructions:
1. Marinate the chicken in lemon juice and salt for half an hour.
2. Cook the onion in a dry pot over medium heat for forty minutes, stirring. It weeps, reduces and turns into a dark paste. Add neither oil nor water.
3. Add the spiced butter, garlic and ginger, cook five minutes, then stir in the berbere and fry five more: the spices have to open in the fat.
4. Pour in the wine and a cup of water, add the chicken and braise covered for forty minutes over a low flame.
5. Score the boiled eggs in several places and slip them into the sauce for the last ten minutes.
6. Serve with injera. The sauce should be thick and dark red, with oil separated on top.

name: Ropa vieja
description: Beef pulled into strands and stewed in sofrito with peppers and olives. The meat is boiled whole in advance.
instructions:
1. Boil the beef whole in salted water with an onion for an hour and a half, until it pulls apart. Keep the broth.
2. Cool it and pull it apart along the grain into thin strands by hand.
3. Sweat the onion and peppers in the olive oil for twenty minutes to complete softness, then add the garlic, cumin and oregano for a minute.
4. Pour in the wine, reduce it by half, add the tomatoes and a cup of the broth. Simmer ten minutes.
5. Return the meat, add the olives and capers and cook another twenty minutes over a low flame. Serve with rice and fried plantain.

name: Jerk chicken
description: Chicken in a marinade of scotch bonnet and allspice, smoked over pimento wood.
instructions:
1. Blend the chillies, allspice, spring onion, thyme, ginger, garlic, soy, lime juice, sugar, nutmeg and oil into a thick paste.
2. Cut deep slashes into the chicken down to the bone and rub the marinade in with gloved hands, filling the cuts.
3. Refrigerate for at least eight hours, better a full day.
4. Bank the coals to one side of the grill and throw soaked allspice berries and wood chips on them. Put the chicken on the far side, away from direct heat.
5. Cook covered at 150-160 °C for an hour and a half, turning every half hour and adding more chips.
6. For the last ten minutes move it over direct heat for colour. Serve with lime and festival bread.

name: Jollof rice
description: Rice cooked in a thick sauce of tomato, pepper and onion. The sauce is reduced dark before the rice goes in.
instructions:
1. Blend the tomatoes, peppers, one onion and the scotch bonnet until smooth.
2. Fry the second onion in the oil until soft, add the tomato paste and cook five minutes, until it darkens.
3. Pour in the purée and reduce it for twenty-five minutes over medium heat, stirring. It darkens, thickens and the oil begins separating at the edges.
4. Add the curry powder, thyme, bay and stock, season and bring it to the boil.
5. Stir in the rinsed rice once, cover with foil and a lid, and cook on the lowest heat for twenty-five minutes. Do not lift the lid or stir.
6. Take it off and let it stand ten minutes. Fork it through from the bottom up, lifting the lower layer.

name: Arepas
description: Cakes of precooked corn flour, griddled and split open to be stuffed.
instructions:
1. Dissolve the salt in the warm water and stir in the flour by hand. Add the butter and cheese.
2. Knead for three minutes and let it stand five. The dough should stop sticking and roll into a ball easily.
3. Shape cakes ten centimetres across and a centimetre and a half thick. Smooth the edges with wet fingers; cracks widen in the pan.
4. Griddle them with a drop of oil for four minutes a side, to a firm crust.
5. Finish them at 180 °C for ten minutes. A done arepa sounds hollow when tapped.
6. Split them hot lengthways, not all the way through, and stuff them: cheese, avocado, stewed meat or egg.

name: Momo
description: Nepali steamed dumplings of buffalo or chicken with an achar of charred tomato.
instructions:
1. Knead a dough from the flour, cold water and a pinch of salt for eight minutes and rest it under film for half an hour.
2. Mix the chopped meat with the onion, ginger, garlic, coriander, timur, a spoon of oil and salt. Do not work it to a paste; pieces should remain.
3. Char the tomatoes over a flame until blackened, toast the chillies and sesame in a dry pan, and blend everything with salt into a sauce.
4. Roll eight-centimetre rounds, thinner at the edges. Add a spoon of filling and pleat all the way round, twisting the top shut.
5. Oil the steamer and cook the momo ten minutes over a fierce steam, keeping them from touching.

name: Kottu roti
description: Godamba roti chopped on the griddle with vegetables, egg and curry, worked with two cleavers.
instructions:
1. Cut the roti into centimetre strips: that makes the chopping easier later.
2. Heat a large pan with the oil, fry the onion, leek and chilli two minutes, add the carrot and cabbage and cook three more.
3. Push the vegetables aside, break the eggs into the cleared space, let them set and break them up.
4. Add the chicken, curry powder and strips of roti and start chopping with two spatulas, mixing as you go. Three minutes of real work.
5. Pour the curry sauce down the side and keep chopping a minute more. The mixture should be moist but not wet.

name: Ćevapi
description: Skinless minced-meat sausages over coals, with raw onion and somun flatbread.
instructions:
1. Combine all three minces with the crushed garlic, bicarbonate, paprika, salt and pepper.
2. Work it by hand for ten minutes, adding the iced water a little at a time, until the mass turns tacky and even.
3. Press film onto the surface and refrigerate for at least twelve hours.
4. With wet hands roll sausages eight centimetres long and as thick as a thumb.
5. Grill over hot coals or on a griddle three minutes a side, turning once.
6. Split the warm somun, tuck the ćevapi inside and add a pile of raw onion and kajmak.

name: Frikadeller
description: Danish meat patties — flat rather than round — fried in butter to a dark crust.
instructions:
1. Mix both minces with the grated onion, egg, flour, salt, pepper and allspice.
2. Work it for five minutes, adding the milk in stages. The mixture should turn tacky and string off the spoon.
3. Chill it for half an hour: cold farce holds its shape better.
4. Melt the butter over medium heat. With a spoon dipped in water, scoop the mixture into the pan and flatten each one.
5. Fry six minutes a side, to a dark brown crust. Do not hurry: the colour is the flavour.
6. Serve with boiled potatoes, pickled red cabbage and the gravy from the pan.

name: Sarmale
description: Cabbage rolls in soured leaves with pork and rice, braised three hours under a layer of shredded cabbage.
instructions:
1. Take the cabbage apart into leaves and pare down the thick ribs. Rinse leaves that are too sour; soak overly salty ones for twenty minutes.
2. Fry the finely chopped onion in the oil until soft, add the tomato paste and cook two minutes. Cool it completely.
3. Mix the pork with the rice, the cooled onion, savory, salt and pepper.
4. Put a tablespoon of filling on each leaf, roll it up and tuck the ends in with a finger. The rolls should come out small, about two fingers wide.
5. Line the pot with shredded cabbage and the ribs, pack the rolls in tight layers with bay between them, and cover with the remaining cabbage and leaves.
6. Add water to the level of the top layer and cook three hours on the lowest heat or at 150 °C in the oven.

name: Shopska salad
description: Tomato, cucumber and pepper under a cap of grated white cheese. The vegetables are cut large, the cheese grated fine.
instructions:
1. Char the peppers over a flame until the skin blackens, close them in a covered dish for ten minutes and peel them.
2. Cut the tomatoes and cucumbers into two-centimetre dice and the peppers into strips.
3. Mix the vegetables with the onion and parsley and dress with the oil, vinegar and salt.
4. Mound it on a dish and blanket it with the grated cheese without stirring. Finish with olives.

name: Lohikeitto
description: Finnish salmon soup with potato and cream, a heap of dill and a knob of butter in the bowl.
instructions:
1. Cover the head and bones with a litre and a half of water, add the allspice and bay, and simmer twenty-five minutes, skimming. Strain it.
2. Fry the leek and carrot in butter for five minutes without letting them colour.
3. Pour in the strained stock, add the potato and cook fifteen minutes until soft.
4. Add the cream and warm it without boiling. Season.
5. Slip in the pieces of salmon and hold them at a bare simmer for exactly five minutes. The fish should stay in whole pieces.
6. Ladle into bowls and add a knob of butter and a generous handful of dill to each.

name: Irish stew
description: Lamb with potato and onion, stewed without browning. The meat is never seared, and that is the whole point.
instructions:
1. Put the meat into the pot raw, add the onion, carrot and the first lot of potatoes cut large.
2. Pour in the stock, bring it to the boil, skim and cook covered for an hour and a half on the lowest heat.
3. Crush the collapsed potato against the side of the pot: the broth thickens and turns milky white.
4. Add the second lot of potatoes in large pieces and cook another forty minutes.
5. Season, and let it stand fifteen minutes. Scatter parsley over before serving.

name: Black risotto
description: Risotto with cuttlefish and its own ink. The ink goes in at the end, or it turns bitter.
instructions:
1. Fry the onion and garlic in olive oil until soft, add the cuttlefish and cook five minutes; it releases water.
2. Add half the wine and the tomato paste and stew covered for twenty-five minutes, topping up with stock, until the cuttlefish softens.
3. Add the rice and toast it two minutes, until the grains turn translucent at the edges. Pour in the rest of the wine.
4. Add hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring, for eighteen minutes. Each addition goes in when the last has nearly been absorbed.
5. Five minutes before the end stir in the ink. The risotto turns black within seconds.
6. Off the heat, beat in a spoon of olive oil and the parsley, cover for two minutes and serve.

name: Gravlaks
description: Salmon cured for two days under a weight with salt, sugar and dill. No heat and no smoke.
instructions:
1. Run your fingers over the fillet for pin bones and pull them with tweezers. Leave the skin on: it holds the shape while curing.
2. Mix the salt, sugar and crushed pepper. Sprinkle the fish with aquavit and rub the mixture into the flesh.
3. Lay half the dill in a dish, the fish on it skin down, and bury it under the rest of the dill.
4. Cover with film, set a board and a kilo weight on top and refrigerate for forty-eight hours.
5. Every twelve hours pour off the brine that has collected and turn the fish over.
6. Scrape off the cure, pat the fish dry and slice it thinly on the diagonal, stopping at the skin. Serve with a mustard sauce of mustard, sugar, vinegar and oil.

name: Moules marinières
description: Mussels steamed in white wine with celery and onion. Five minutes under a lid, no longer.
instructions:
1. Sort the mussels: discard any that are cracked or that will not close when tapped. Pull away the beards and rinse them under the tap.
2. Melt the butter in a wide pot and sweat the shallot, celery and garlic for five minutes without letting them colour.
3. Pour in the wine, add the thyme and bay and bring it to the boil.
4. Tip in the mussels, cover at once and hold them over a fierce flame for five minutes, shaking the pot a couple of times.
5. Lift the lid: the shells should be open. Throw out any that are not. Scatter parsley, add pepper and serve with chips and the broth in a separate cup.

name: Cheese fondue
description: Gruyère and Vacherin melted in white wine with starch. The acidity of the wine keeps the cheese from seizing.
instructions:
1. Rub the inside of the pot with a cut clove of garlic and leave it in.
2. Toss both grated cheeses with the cornflour by hand until every shred is coated.
3. Warm the wine with the lemon juice until bubbles appear at the edge, but not to a boil.
4. Add the cheese a handful at a time, stirring in a figure of eight until each is fully melted before the next goes in.
5. When the mass turns even and strings from the spoon, add the kirsch and season with nutmeg and pepper.
6. Move it to the burner and keep the flame at its lowest. The bread is speared through the crust rather than the crumb.

name: Ghapama
description: A whole pumpkin baked with rice, dried fruit and nuts. A festive dish, cut open at the table.
instructions:
1. Cut the top off the pumpkin with its stalk; that is the lid. Scoop out the seeds and loose flesh with a spoon, leaving a wall two fingers thick.
2. Boil the rice in salted water for seven minutes, to half done, and drain.
3. Cover the dried fruit with boiling water for ten minutes, drain, and chop the apricots and prunes coarsely. Chop the nuts.
4. Mix the rice with the fruit, nuts, melted butter, honey and cinnamon. Salt it: a sweet filling without salt tastes flat.
5. Fill the pumpkin, without packing it down, put the cut lid back on and set it on a baking tray.
6. Bake at 180 °C for an hour and a half. Test at the side with a knife: it should go into the wall without resistance.
7. Rest fifteen minutes, carry it out whole and cut it into wedges from the crown to the base.

name: Shah plov
description: Pilaf baked in a crown of lavash. The crust holds its shape and is cut in wedges like a pie.
instructions:
1. Soak the rice in salted water for an hour, then boil it seven minutes in plenty of water and drain.
2. Steep the saffron in three spoons of boiling water and leave it; it gives both colour and scent.
3. Brown the lamb, add the onion and cook until soft. Add the chestnuts, apricots, raisins and turmeric and stew for twenty minutes.
4. Butter a deep dish generously and line it with overlapping lavash, letting the edges hang outside.
5. Layer it: rice, filling, rice again. Pour over the saffron infusion and the rest of the butter.
6. Fold the lavash edges over the top, cover with foil and bake at 180 °C for forty minutes, then uncover and give it fifteen more to colour.
7. Rest ten minutes, cover with a platter and invert. Cut it at the table.

name: Beshbarmak
description: Boiled meat on sheets of pasta with an onion broth called sorpa. The centrepiece of a Kazakh table.
instructions:
1. Cover the meat with cold water, bring it up, skim, and simmer on the lowest heat for two and a half hours with the peppercorns and bay.
2. Knead a stiff dough from the flour, eggs, water and salt and rest it under film for forty minutes.
3. Roll the dough a millimetre thick and cut it into squares of about eight centimetres.
4. Slice the onion into rings, pour a ladle of hot broth over it and leave it ten minutes; this is the sorpa that dresses the dish.
5. Lift out the meat, skim the fat into a separate bowl and boil the dough squares in that broth in batches, three to four minutes each.
6. Pull the meat apart into thin sheets across the grain. Lay the dough on a large platter, the meat on top, the onions and their broth over that.
7. Serve the remaining broth hot in bowls with herbs; it is drunk before the dish or alongside it.

name: Bryndzové halušky
description: Potato dumplings with sheep's brynza and bacon crackling. Slovakia's national dish.
instructions:
1. Grate the potatoes finely and squeeze them lightly; only a little water should go, as a dry mass will not bind.
2. Mix in the flour, egg and salt. The mass should slide off a spoon slowly rather than pour.
3. Fry the bacon in a dry pan until crisp and lift it out, keeping the fat.
4. Push the dough into boiling salted water through a colander with large holes. The dumplings are done when they float, after about three minutes.
5. Drain the dumplings, return them to the warm pan and stir in the brynza with a spoon of the cooking water. Keep the heat off.
6. Serve into bowls, spoon over the hot fat and scatter the crackling on top.

name: Pastel de choclo
description: A bake of meat filling under a lid of ground sweetcorn, with an olive and an egg inside.
instructions:
1. Fry the finely chopped onion until translucent, add the mince, cumin, salt and pepper and cook through. Let the pino cool; warm, it will weep.
2. Blitz the corn with the basil and milk to a coarse but even mass.
3. Cook it down with the butter over medium heat, stirring, for about fifteen minutes, until a spoon stands up in it.
4. Divide the pino between earthenware dishes and top each with a piece of chicken, half an egg and a couple of olives with raisins.
5. Cover with a two-centimetre layer of the corn mass, level it and dust with sugar.
6. Bake at 200 °C for forty minutes, the last five under the grill, to a dark caramel crust.

name: Pabellón criollo
description: A plate in four parts: shredded stewed beef, black beans, white rice and fried plantain.
instructions:
1. Boil the beans with half the onion and some garlic until soft, an hour to ninety minutes. Salt at the end.
2. Simmer the beef whole in salted water for an hour and twenty minutes. Lift it out and cool it enough to handle.
3. Pull the meat into threads along the grain. Across the grain it shreds into crumbs.
4. Fry the remaining onion, pepper and garlic, add the tomatoes and cumin, then the meat, and stew twenty minutes with a ladle of the broth.
5. Cook the rice loose, without butter or spice; here it is the neutral part.
6. Slice the plantain on the diagonal and fry over medium heat until caramel on both sides.
7. Build the plate in sectors: rice, beans, meat and plantain side by side, unmixed.

name: Salteñas
description: Baked pastries whose filling stays liquid inside. The Bolivian mid-morning snack.
instructions:
1. Fry the onion with the ají and cumin, add the beef and cook through. Pour in the stock and simmer ten minutes.
2. Dissolve the gelatine in a couple of spoons of hot water and stir it into the stew with the potato and peas.
3. Cool the filling and refrigerate it for at least four hours; it has to set to a firm jelly.
4. Knead a dough from the flour, softened butter, sugar, achiote, salt and warm water. Rest it half an hour.
5. Roll fifteen-centimetre rounds. On each go a spoon of the cold jelly, a wedge of egg and an olive.
6. Seal the seam in a plait along the top and stand the pastries seam-up. Any gap means the broth escapes.
7. Bake at 220 °C for twenty-five minutes. The high heat is what sets the pastry before the jelly melts.

name: Encebollado
description: A tuna soup with cassava and pickled onion. Ecuadorians eat it for breakfast and treat it as a hangover cure.
instructions:
1. Cure the onion in the juice of two limes with salt and leave it at least fifteen minutes.
2. Fry the garlic and tomatoes with the cumin for five minutes, add a litre and a half of water and bring it up.
3. Lower in the tuna whole and poach it fifteen minutes on a low heat. Fish does not tolerate a hard boil.
4. Lift out the fish, strain the broth and return it to the heat. Cook the cassava in it for twenty minutes, until soft.
5. Flake the tuna coarsely, discarding the dark parts, and return it to the pot for two minutes.
6. Ladle it out and top with the cured onion and its juice and coriander. Serve with a wedge of lime.

name: Masgouf
description: River fish butterflied and cooked standing beside an open fire. A Baghdad dish from the banks of the Tigris.
instructions:
1. Cut the fish along the back without separating the belly, gut it and open it out like a book. Leave the spine in.
2. Mix the oil, turmeric, tamarind, curry powder, salt and pepper and paint the flesh with it. Leave the skin alone.
3. Leave the fish half an hour at room temperature; cold, it cooks unevenly.
4. Light the fire and let it settle to a steady flame. Stand the fish upright, flesh towards the fire, half a metre away.
5. Cook for an hour, turning as needed. The flesh should whiten and dry at the edges without scorching.
6. Move the fish skin down onto the coals, lay the onion and tomato over it and give it ten more minutes.
7. Serve it on the board, with flatbread, lemon and raw onion.

name: Mansaf
description: Lamb in a sauce of jameed, fermented dried yoghurt, over rice and flatbread. Jordan's national dish.
instructions:
1. Soak the jameed in warm water for four hours, break it up by hand and pass it through a sieve to an even liquid.
2. Simmer the lamb with the cardamom for an hour and twenty minutes, skimming. Keep the broth.
3. Pour the jameed liquid in with the meat and bring it up, stirring continuously in one direction.
4. Drop the heat to its lowest and hold it forty minutes. The sauce thickens and turns creamy.
5. Cook the rice in the meat broth with turmeric and a spoon of ghee.
6. Fry the almonds and pine nuts in ghee until golden and set them aside.
7. Line a platter with the bread, moisten it with sauce, spread the rice, lay the meat on top, spoon over more sauce and scatter the nuts and parsley.

name: Brik
description: A thin sheet of pastry with an egg inside, fried so the yolk stays liquid.
instructions:
1. Mix the mashed potato with the tuna, chopped onion, capers, parsley, harissa, salt and pepper.
2. Heat the oil to 180 °C. Test with a scrap of pastry: it should surface at once and sizzle.
3. Lay a sheet on a plate, put two spoons of filling on one half and make a hollow in it.
4. Break an egg into the hollow, season it and fold the sheet over immediately, pressing the edges.
5. Slide the brik into the oil and fry forty seconds a side, steadying it with a slotted spoon.
6. Drain on paper and serve immediately with a wedge of lemon.

name: Algerian couscous
description: Semolina steamed three times over a pot of meat and vegetables, with the broth served apart.
instructions:
1. Brown the meat with the onion in the base of the couscoussier, add the tomato paste, spices and chickpeas and cover with water. Cook an hour.
2. Sprinkle the couscous with water and oil and rub it between your hands so the grains separate. Steam it fifteen minutes.
3. Turn the grain into a wide dish, sprinkle again, rake it apart and let it cool five minutes.
4. Return it to the steam for fifteen more minutes. Meanwhile add the carrot and turnip to the broth.
5. Rake it a third time, working in the butter, and steam it a final ten minutes.
6. Add the courgette and pumpkin to the broth for the last twenty minutes; they cook faster than the roots.
7. Mound the couscous, meat and vegetables on top. Serve the broth in a separate bowl and the harissa in a third.

name: Cepelinai
description: Large potato dumplings with a meat filling, named after airships. Served with crackling and soured cream.
instructions:
1. Grate the raw potato finely and wring it out in a cloth. Collect the liquid in a bowl.
2. Let the liquid stand ten minutes, pour off the water and stir the settled starch back into the grated potato.
3. Mash the boiled potato and combine it with the grated, adding the starch and salt. The mass should shape without sticking.
4. Mix the mince with half the finely chopped onion, marjoram, salt and pepper and roll four firm balls.
5. With wet hands take a lump of dough, flatten it on your palm, set the filling in it and seal it into an elongated oval.
6. Lower them into barely simmering salted water and cook twenty-five minutes. Do not stir; just rock the pot once in the first minute.
7. Render the pork fat with the remaining onion to crackling, spoon it over the cepelinai and serve with soured cream.

name: Grey peas with speck
description: Grey peas cooked soft with onion and rendered smoked pork. Latvian winter and Christmas food.
instructions:
1. Soak the peas twelve hours in cold water, changing it once.
2. Drain, cover with fresh water two fingers above and boil unsalted for an hour and twenty minutes, until soft.
3. Dice the pork belly and render it in a dry pan to golden crackling.
4. Add the chopped onion and fry it in the rendered fat until soft and golden.
5. Drain the peas, leaving a little liquid in the pot, and season with salt and pepper.
6. Stir the crackling, onion and fat into the peas and serve hot, with cold kefir in a glass.

name: Mulgipuder
description: A mash of potato and pearl barley with pork crackling. An Estonian dish recognised as a national symbol.
instructions:
1. Rinse the barley and boil it in salted water for an hour, until soft.
2. Add the roughly cut potato to the same pot and cook twenty minutes more.
3. Render the pork belly to crackling, add the onion and fry until golden.
4. Drain most of the water from the barley and potato, keeping half a cup.
5. Mash with the butter and milk, leaving the barley grains still visible. Season with salt and pepper.
6. Serve into bowls and spoon the crackling, onion and rendered fat over the top.

name: Draniki
description: Potato pancakes from raw grated potato, fried to a crisp edge and served with soured cream.
instructions:
1. Grate the potato and onion finely into the same bowl.
2. Let the mass stand three minutes and pour off the water that gathers on top, leaving the sediment.
3. Season with salt and pepper. Add nothing else.
4. Heat the oil over medium and drop the mixture in by the spoonful, flattening it to half a centimetre.
5. Fry three to four minutes a side, to a deep golden crisp crust.
6. Drain on paper and serve immediately with soured cream and dill.

name: Mohinga
description: Rice noodles in a thick fish broth built on banana stem. Breakfast, and Myanmar's unofficial national dish.
instructions:
1. Poach the fish with the lemongrass and turmeric for fifteen minutes, lift it out and pick the flesh, discarding bones and skin. Strain the broth.
2. Pound the onion, garlic and ginger to a paste and fry it in oil with the paprika until dark and fragrant.
3. Mash the fish with a fork and stir it into the paste, frying five minutes; it should break down into threads.
4. Transfer everything to the pot with the broth, add the fish sauce and simmer twenty minutes.
5. Slake the rice and chickpea flours in cold water to a thin slurry and pour it into the soup in a stream, stirring.
6. Cook twenty minutes more, until the broth thickens to the consistency of thin cream.
7. Boil the noodles, divide them between bowls, ladle the soup over and serve with egg, split peas, coriander and lime.

name: Fish amok
description: Fish in a coconut curry, steamed in a cup folded from banana leaf.
instructions:
1. Pound the lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, garlic, shallot and half the lime leaves in a mortar to a smooth paste.
2. Warm the paste in a pan with half the coconut milk for five minutes, until it smells right.
3. Take it off the heat, cool it to warm and whisk in the eggs, fish sauce, palm sugar and the rest of the milk.
4. Fold the fish pieces through and leave them to marinate fifteen minutes.
5. Fold cups from the banana leaves, or use ramekins. Line the bottom with spinach leaves.
6. Divide the fish and sauce between them without filling to the brim and steam for twenty minutes.
7. Spoon over the coconut cream, scatter with shredded lime leaves and serve with rice.

name: Hainanese chicken rice
description: A whole chicken poached below boiling and rice cooked in its broth, with three sauces.
instructions:
1. Rub the chicken with salt inside and out and stuff the cavity with half the ginger and the spring onions.
2. Bring a pot of water to the boil, lower the whole chicken in, bring it back up and turn the heat off immediately.
3. Keep it covered for forty minutes without lifting the lid. It is done when the juices from the thigh run clear.
4. Move the chicken into iced water for ten minutes, then pat it dry and brush it with sesame oil.
5. Skim the fat from the broth, fry the chopped garlic and ginger in it, add the rinsed rice and toast it three minutes.
6. Add broth to the rice at one and a half to one, drop in the pandan leaf and cook covered for fifteen minutes.
7. Pound the chillies with garlic, ginger and lime into a sauce. Joint the chicken and serve with the rice, cucumber, sauce and a bowl of the broth.

name: Lu rou fan
description: Minced pork belly braised in soy sauce with spices, spooned over white rice.
instructions:
1. Dice the belly into one-centimetre cubes, keeping the fat with the meat.
2. Fry the sliced shallots in oil to a deep golden crisp and set half aside for serving.
3. In the same oil brown the pork, rendering some of its fat, for ten minutes.
4. Add the wine, let it cook off for a minute, then add both soy sauces, the sugar, spices and garlic.
5. Add water level with the meat, bring it up and braise covered for ninety minutes on the lowest heat.
6. Add the boiled eggs to the sauce for the last twenty minutes; they take on the colour and flavour.
7. Serve over rice with half an egg, blanched greens and the fried shallots on top.

name: Nyama choma
description: Goat meat grilled slowly over coals in large pieces, with kachumbari and ugali.
instructions:
1. Rub the meat with salt, pepper, the juice of two lemons, crushed garlic and oil. Leave it an hour.
2. Light the coals and let them ash over. The heat is right when you can hold a palm above the grate for five seconds.
3. Lay the meat on in whole pieces and grill, turning every ten minutes, for an hour and twenty.
4. Mix the diced tomato, onion, coriander and chilli with lemon juice and salt; that is kachumbari.
5. For the ugali bring a litre of water to the boil, rain in the flour, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, and work it fifteen minutes into a firm mass.
6. Rest the meat ten minutes, cut it small across the grain and serve with ugali, kachumbari and salt.

name: Waakye
description: Rice and black-eyed beans cooked with sorghum leaves, which turn it deep red.
instructions:
1. Rinse the sorghum leaves and boil them in a litre and a half of water for ten minutes; the water turns deep red.
2. Take the leaves out, add a pinch of soda and the beans and cook forty-five minutes, until nearly done.
3. Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and add it to the pot. The liquid should stand a finger above the rice.
4. Salt it, cover and cook twenty minutes on a low heat without stirring.
5. Take it off the heat, leave it covered ten minutes, then fluff it with a fork.
6. Fry slices of ripe plantain until caramel-coloured.
7. Serve with egg, gari, shito and plantain, all on one plate.

name: Thieboudienne
description: Rice cooked in the tomato broth from the fish, with herb-stuffed fish and vegetables. Senegal's national dish.
instructions:
1. Pound the parsley, garlic, chilli and salt into the rof paste and press it into slashes cut in the fish.
2. Fry the fish three minutes a side and set it aside.
3. In the same oil fry the onion until soft, add the tomato paste and cook five minutes, until it darkens.
4. Add two litres of water, the tamarind and the vegetables and cook twenty-five minutes.
5. Return the fish to the pot for ten minutes, then lift it and the vegetables out and keep them warm.
6. Add the rinsed rice to the remaining broth — twice as much liquid as rice — and cook covered for thirty minutes without stirring.
7. Turn the rice onto a large platter with the fish and vegetables on top. Share out the caught layer from the bottom separately.

name: Bobotie
description: A bake of spiced mince with dried fruit under an egg and milk custard. South Africa's national dish.
instructions:
1. Soak the bread in half the milk for ten minutes and squeeze it out, keeping the milk.
2. Fry the onion in oil until soft, add the curry powder and turmeric and warm them a minute, until fragrant.
3. Add the mince and cook, breaking up lumps, until it loses its pink, about ten minutes.
4. Stir in the bread, apricots, raisins, chutney, vinegar, salt and pepper and take it off the heat.
5. Press it into a dish, level it and bake at 180 °C for forty minutes.
6. Beat the eggs with the remaining milk, pour it over, stand the bay leaves in the custard and scatter the almonds.
7. Return it to the oven for twenty minutes, until the custard sets and turns golden.

name: Plokkfiskur
description: Flaked boiled fish mashed with potato in a white sauce. Icelandic home cooking made from leftovers.
instructions:
1. Boil the potatoes in their skins until tender, peel them and cut them into large pieces.
2. Poach the cod in salted water for eight minutes, lift it out and flake it by hand, removing bones and skin.
3. Fry the onion in butter until soft, stir in the flour and cook it two minutes, stirring.
4. Pour in the milk in a thin stream, whisking continuously, and bring the sauce to the thickness of cream.
5. Stir in the mustard, salt and pepper, add the fish and potato and warm everything through for five minutes.
6. Mash with a fork to a coarse, uneven texture in which the pieces are still recognisable, and scatter with chives.

name: Potica
description: A yeasted roll with a walnut filling, coiled into a ring. Slovenian baking for every celebration.
instructions:
1. Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk with a spoon of sugar and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
2. Knead a dough from the flour, the yeast mixture, yolks, sugar, softened butter, zest and salt. Work it fifteen minutes.
3. Leave it somewhere warm for an hour and twenty, until it has doubled.
4. Warm the cream with the honey, pour it over the ground walnuts, add the rum and cinnamon and cool it to lukewarm.
5. Roll the dough into a rectangle three millimetres thick and spread the filling, leaving two centimetres clear at the edges.
6. Roll it up tightly from the long side, lay it in a ring tin seam down and let it prove forty minutes.
7. Prick the roll in several places with a skewer and bake at 170 °C for an hour, to a deep gold.

name: Bosanski lonac
description: Meat and vegetables layered in a clay pot and cooked four hours without stirring.
instructions:
1. Cut all the vegetables into large pieces; they have to survive four hours without collapsing.
2. Line the bottom of the pot with the diced pork fat, put the meat on it and season.
3. Layer on the onion, carrot, parsley root, potato, peppers, cabbage and tomato.
4. Tuck in the whole head of garlic and the bay leaves, pour in the wine and add water to half the height of the pot.
5. Cover and put it in a 150 °C oven for four hours. Do not open it and do not stir.
6. Serve straight from the pot, digging to the bottom so every layer reaches the plate.

name: Tavče gravče
description: White beans baked in a clay pan with onion, paprika and peppers. North Macedonia's national dish.
instructions:
1. Drain the soaked beans, cover them with fresh water, bring it to the boil and drain again after ten minutes.
2. Cover them a third time, add one whole onion and boil an hour until soft, without salt.
3. Fry the sliced onion in oil until golden, take it off the heat and stir in the paprika and flour.
4. Pour off some of the bean water, leaving it level with the beans, salt them and stir in the onion mixture.
5. Transfer to a clay pan, arrange the dried peppers on top and scatter with mint.
6. Bake at 200 °C for forty minutes, until a browned crust forms on top.
7. Rest ten minutes and serve straight from the pan, scattered with parsley.

name: Lamingtons
description: Cubes of sponge dipped in chocolate icing and rolled in desiccated coconut.
instructions:
1. Beat the butter and sugar pale, add the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla.
2. Fold in the sifted flour with the baking powder and salt, alternating with the milk.
3. Pour into a square tin and bake at 180 °C for twenty-eight minutes, until a skewer comes out clean.
4. Cool it completely and leave the sponge uncovered overnight.
5. Cut it into five-centimetre cubes.
6. Whisk the icing sugar with the cocoa and hot milk to a thin icing that runs off a spoon in a stream.
7. Dip each cube on two forks, let it drain and roll it in coconut. Leave them to set for an hour.

name: Pavlova
description: A meringue with a crisp shell and a marshmallow centre, under whipped cream and kiwifruit.
instructions:
1. Whisk room-temperature egg whites to soft peaks in a scrupulously dry, grease-free bowl.
2. Add the sugar a spoonful at a time, still whisking, until the meringue is stiff and glossy.
3. Rub some between your fingers: if you feel sugar grains, keep going, or the shell will weep syrup.
4. Fold in the cornflour, vinegar and vanilla with a spatula, in three movements at most.
5. Shape a twenty-two centimetre circle on parchment, raising the edges and leaving a hollow in the middle.
6. Bake at 120 °C for ninety minutes, then turn the oven off and leave the pavlova inside until completely cold.
7. Whip the cream, spoon it into the hollow and top with kiwifruit, berries and passionfruit pulp just before serving.

name: Poutine
description: Chips with cheese curds under hot gravy. The Québécois street classic.
instructions:
1. Cut the potatoes into one-centimetre batons and soak them twenty minutes in cold water to lose the surface starch.
2. Dry the batons thoroughly. Wet potato spits in the fryer and never crusts.
3. Melt the butter, stir in the flour and cook the roux to a nutty brown, four minutes.
4. Add both stocks, the Worcestershire sauce and the vinegar and simmer the gravy fifteen minutes, until thick.
5. Fry the potatoes at 150 °C for six minutes, until soft, and drain them on a rack.
6. Bring the oil to 190 °C and fry them a second time for three minutes, to a crisp shell. Salt them.
7. Pile the chips into a bowl, scatter the curds over them and pour on the boiling gravy. Serve at once.

name: Gallo pinto
description: Yesterday's rice fried with black beans and Salsa Lizano. The Costa Rican breakfast, every day.
instructions:
1. Fry the finely chopped onion, pepper and garlic in oil until soft, five minutes.
2. Add the beans with a ladle of their liquid and warm them three minutes.
3. Add the cold rice and stir, breaking up lumps with a spatula.
4. Add the Salsa Lizano, season and fry over medium heat for seven minutes, stirring occasionally.
5. Stir in the chopped coriander and take it off the heat.
6. Serve with fried eggs, fried plantain and, if you like, soured cream or fresh cheese.

name: Buuz
description: Large steamed dumplings of chopped mutton. The centrepiece of the Mongolian lunar new year.
instructions:
1. Knead a stiff dough from the flour, water and salt and rest it under film for forty minutes.
2. Chop the mutton and fat by hand into pieces the size of a pea.
3. Mix the meat with the finely chopped onion, garlic, salt, pepper and a quarter cup of water.
4. Roll ten-centimetre rounds, leaving the middle thicker than the edges.
5. Put a spoon of filling in and pleat the edges around, leaving an opening at the top.
6. Grease the steamer rack with fat and set the buuz on it, not touching one another.
7. Steam eighteen minutes. The dough turns translucent and broth collects inside.

name: Kyrgyz beshbarmak
description: Mutton with home-made noodles in an onion sauce called chyk. The Kyrgyz version: mutton, and no potato.
instructions:
1. Cover the meat with cold water, bring it up, skim and simmer two and a half hours with the peppercorns and bay.
2. Knead a stiff dough from the flour, eggs, water and salt and rest it forty minutes.
3. Roll it a millimetre thick and cut it into diamonds six centimetres across.
4. Render the mutton fat and cook the sliced onion in it until soft.
5. Add two ladles of broth to the onion and stew ten minutes into a thick gravy; that is the chyk.
6. Boil the dough diamonds in the strained broth in batches, four minutes each, and plate them straight away.
7. Pull the meat into sheets, lay it over the dough, spoon the chyk over and scatter with coriander. Serve the broth in bowls.

name: Qurutob
description: Flaky fatir bread soaked in reconstituted dried qurut, under fried onion and fresh vegetables.
instructions:
1. Cover the qurut with hot water for twenty minutes and rub it by hand into an even liquid.
2. Pass it through a sieve to remove any grains. The liquid should be like thin soured cream.
3. Slice the onion into rings and fry it in oil until golden, ten minutes.
4. Tear the fatir into large pieces into a wide dish.
5. Pour the qurut over the bread and leave it five minutes to soak.
6. Top with the fried onion and its oil, then the tomato, cucumber and herbs.

name: Kabuli pulao
description: Rice with lamb under a layer of caramelised carrot, raisins and almonds. Afghanistan's national dish.
instructions:
1. Soak the rice in salted water for two hours and rinse it until the water runs clear.
2. Fry the onion in oil until deep gold, add the meat and brown it.
3. Add a litre of water, the cardamom and salt and simmer an hour, until the meat is tender. Strain the broth.
4. Melt two spoons of sugar in a dry pan to a dark caramel and let it down carefully with a ladle of broth.
5. Fry the carrot with the rest of the sugar for five minutes until glossy, add the raisins and nuts and take it off.
6. Parboil the rice for five minutes and drain it.
7. Layer the rice over the meat in the pot, spoon over the caramel broth, dust with char masala, pierce to the bottom and hold covered thirty minutes on a low heat. Serve with the carrot and raisins on top.

name: Fattoush
description: A salad of vegetables and herbs with fried pieces of flatbread and sumac.
instructions:
1. Tear the bread by hand into two-finger pieces and fry them in olive oil until browned.
2. Drain the bread on paper and dust it with half the sumac while it is still hot.
3. Cut the tomatoes, cucumbers and radishes into large uneven pieces; the salad should be rough rather than neat.
4. Tear the lettuce by hand and chop the herbs and spring onion.
5. Whisk a dressing from the lemon juice, pomegranate molasses, crushed garlic, the remaining sumac, oil and salt.
6. Toss the vegetables in the dressing, add the bread and serve at once.

name: Shuwa
description: Lamb in a spice paste, wrapped in leaves and cooked for a full day. Oman's dish for Eid.
instructions:
1. Grind the garlic, all the spices, the crushed dried limes, vinegar, oil and salt into a thick paste.
2. Cut deep slashes to the bone and rub the paste inside them and all over the outside.
3. Refrigerate overnight, twelve hours at least.
4. Wrap the meat in banana leaves, then tightly in two layers of foil. No gap may remain.
5. Set the parcel on a tray, pour a cup of water into the tray and bake at 130 °C for eight hours.
6. Unwrap it, pour off the juices and cook the rice in them. Pull the meat into threads by hand.
7. Serve the meat over the rice, from a shared platter, eaten by hand.

name: Sudanese ful
description: Ful beans cooked soft and mashed in the pot, with sesame oil, cheese and egg.
instructions:
1. Drain the soaked beans, cover them with fresh water and boil ninety minutes, until completely soft.
2. Pour off most of the water, leaving half a cup, salt the beans and mash them about halfway.
3. Crush the garlic with salt and cumin and stir it through the beans.
4. Turn them into a wide bowl and pour the sesame oil over without stirring it in.
5. Scatter over the crumbled cheese, chopped tomato, onion, chilli and halved eggs.
6. Serve with lemon and flatbread. It is eaten by hand from the shared bowl.

name: Zanzibar pilau
description: Rice with beef on the island's spices: clove, cardamom, cinnamon and black pepper, and no turmeric at all.
instructions:
1. Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it twenty minutes.
2. Simmer the beef with half the spices for forty minutes, until tender. Keep the broth.
3. Fry the onion in oil over medium heat for twenty minutes, to a deep brown, almost black.
4. Add the garlic, ginger and the remaining spices and warm them two minutes.
5. Add the cooked meat and the diced potato, stir and warm through five minutes.
6. Add the rice, pour in broth at one and a half times the volume of the rice, and season.
7. Bring it up, cover and cook twenty minutes on a low heat without lifting the lid. Rest it ten minutes.

name: Shorshe ilish
description: Hilsa in a ground mustard sauce, cooked by steaming. The great fish of Bengal.
instructions:
1. Soak the mustard seeds in warm water for twenty minutes.
2. Grind them with two chillies, a pinch of salt and a little water into a smooth paste.
3. Rub the fish steaks with turmeric and salt and leave them ten minutes.
4. Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, take it off and let it cool a minute; raw mustard oil is acrid.
5. Add the nigella, pour in the mustard paste let down with half a cup of water, and cook three minutes.
6. Lay the fish in a single layer, add the remaining chillies whole, cover and stew twelve minutes.
7. Finish with a spoon of raw mustard oil, take it off the heat and serve with rice.

name: Larb
description: Chopped meat with toasted rice powder, herbs and lime. The national dish of Laos.
instructions:
1. Toast the raw sticky rice in a dry pan for ten minutes, to a deep gold, stirring.
2. Grind the cooled rice in a mortar or mill to a coarse powder.
3. Chop the pork fine with a knife, but not to a paste; the pieces should stay distinguishable.
4. Cook the meat in a pan with two spoons of water over medium heat for five minutes, breaking up lumps.
5. Take it off the heat and let it cool to warm, about five minutes.
6. Stir in the fish sauce, lime juice, chilli, shallot and rice powder.
7. Add the herbs, toss and serve with sticky rice and raw vegetables.

name: Souvla
description: Large pieces of pork or lamb on a spit, turning slowly over coals for two hours.
instructions:
1. Cut the meat into large pieces of about two hundred grams, keeping the fat; it is needed.
2. Salt and pepper them generously all over and leave them half an hour at room temperature.
3. Light the coals and rake them to the sides, leaving the centre clear. Direct heat under the meat is not wanted.
4. Thread the pieces onto the spit, leaving a centimetre between them.
5. Turn the spit slowly and continuously for two hours. The meat should darken gradually rather than crust at once.
6. Dust with oregano ten minutes before the end and squeeze lemon over.
7. Take it off, cut it coarsely and serve in pita with onion, tomato and parsley.

name: Maltese rabbit stew
description: Rabbit stewed in red wine with garlic and bay. The national dish of Malta.
instructions:
1. Cover the jointed rabbit with the wine, half the garlic and the bay leaves and refrigerate for a day.
2. Lift out the meat, dry it and brown it in olive oil. Keep the marinade.
3. Fry the onion and remaining garlic until soft, add the tomato paste and cook three minutes.
4. Return the meat, pour in the marinade, season and stew covered for an hour on a low heat.
5. Add the potato and carrot and stew twenty-five minutes more.
6. Add the peas for the last ten minutes.
7. Ladle off some of the sauce and dress spaghetti with it as a first course. The meat follows.

name: Chivito
description: A sandwich of thin steak, ham, bacon, cheese and a fried egg. Uruguay's national dish.
instructions:
1. Pound the beef under film to four millimetres and season it.
2. Fry the bacon crisp and drain it on paper.
3. Get the pan very hot and sear the steaks forty-five seconds a side.
4. Lay the cheese on the meat in the pan and cover it for thirty seconds so it softens.
5. Fry the eggs with runny yolks and toast the cut buns in a dry pan.
6. Spread mayonnaise on both halves and layer lettuce, tomato, the steak with its cheese, ham, bacon and the egg.
7. Close it, spear it with a cocktail stick and an olive, and serve with chips.
